summary.title: Systems Benchmarking Crimes
summary.one_liner: A catalogue of common benchmarking mistakes in systems research, such as biased benchmark subsets, misreported overheads, and wrong averaging, each paired with the honest alternative.
keywords: throughput overhead cpu cost per bit
takeaways: Evaluate both the performance gain and any degradation elsewhere; report trade-offs rather than only favourable scenarios.
Do not quote an overall average from a SPEC subset, and justify every omitted program.
Compute overhead correctly: use the original system as the baseline denominator, distinguish percentage points from percentage change, and consider CPU cost per bit for throughput comparisons.
Quote variance (e.g. standard deviation) or significance tests, and use the geometric mean rather than the arithmetic mean to combine normalised scores.

Use a proper baseline (native system, state of the art, or theoretical optimum), keep calibration and validation data disjoint, and fully specify the evaluation platform and competitor configurations.
summary.summary: Gernot Heiser's opinion-driven checklist lists recurring evaluation faults in systems papers, grouped into selective benchmarking, improper handling of results, misleading benchmarks, improper baselines and missing information. Each entry gives a short example, often drawn from real reviewing experience, and explains why it misleads. The page recommends concrete fixes, such as reporting the full CPU load for throughput comparisons, using the geometric mean for summary scores, and comparing against native or state-of-the-art baselines. It is a work-in-progress list, and the last section (missing platform specification) is cut off in the provided text.
